reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard haematology references
clinicalPearls: An inherited pure red cell aplasia usually presenting within the first year of life with severe macrocytic anaemia and reticulocytopenia
It is a ribosomopathy, most commonly caused by heterozygous mutations in ribosomal protein genes such as RPS19
The marrow shows a selective near-absence of erythroid precursors with normal granulocytic and megakaryocytic lineages
Congenital anomalies occur in a substantial minority, including craniofacial (Cathie facies), thumb (triphalangeal or duplicated), cardiac, and genitourinary malformations, and short stature
Biochemical clues include raised erythrocyte adenosine deaminase activity and elevated fetal haemoglobin
Management principles are corticosteroids, to which many patients respond, chronic transfusion with iron chelation for non-responders, and allogeneic stem cell transplantation as a curative option
There is an increased long-term risk of myelodysplastic syndrome, acute leukaemia and certain solid tumours, warranting surveillance
It must be distinguished from transient erythroblastopenia of childhood, which is self-limiting, occurs in older infants, and is usually normocytic
Chronic transfusion carries a substantial burden of iron overload requiring monitoring and chelation
reference.pathophysiology: Diamond-Blackfan anaemia is a congenital ribosomopathy in which heterozygous mutations in genes encoding ribosomal proteins (or, less often, other ribosome-associated factors) impair ribosome biogenesis. Defective ribosomal assembly is thought to trigger stabilisation of p53 and increased apoptosis that selectively affects the highly proliferative erythroid progenitors, producing a profound failure of red cell production while other lineages are largely spared. The same ribosomal and p53-related mechanisms are believed to contribute to the associated congenital malformations and to the predisposition to malignancy.
additionalDifferentials: Parvovirus B19-induced red cell aplasia (especially with underlying haemolysis)
Other inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (Fanconi anaemia, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with reticulocyte count showing macrocytic anaemia and reticulocytopenia
Bone marrow examination demonstrating selective erythroid hypoplasia
Erythrocyte adenosine deaminase activity and fetal haemoglobin level
Molecular genetic testing of ribosomal protein genes
Iron studies and organ iron assessment in transfused patients
redFlags: Severe symptomatic anaemia requiring urgent transfusion
Emergence of new cytopenias, dysplasia or blasts suggesting transformation to MDS or leukaemia
Complications of transfusional iron overload affecting heart, liver or endocrine organs
Development of an associated solid tumour
Loss of steroid responsiveness with transfusion dependence
reference.prognosis: Many patients achieve durable steroid responsiveness or remission, and stem cell transplantation can cure the anaemia, but transfusion-dependent patients face cumulative iron overload and all patients carry an elevated risk of clonal evolution and malignancy. Overall outcome depends on treatment response, transfusion burden and emergence of MDS, leukaemia or solid tumours.
pitfalls: Confusing it with transient erythroblastopenia of childhood and mismanaging accordingly
Failing to monitor and chelate iron in transfusion-dependent patients
Overlooking associated congenital anomalies and the malignancy risk
Missing parvovirus B19 as a treatable alternative cause of red cell aplasia
Neglecting long-term surveillance for clonal evolution
